thread.title: CNBC's Cramer says stocks are 'opening up huge on nothing', sees signs of 'classic bear market'

author: morningstar.com
title: CNBC's Cramer says stocks are 'opening up huge on nothing', sees signs of 'classic bear market'
text:
By Mark DeCambre, MarketWatch
Dow poised for best gain in about 3 weeks
Are we in bear market or something more benign?
That is the crucial question bedeviling a number of investors, including CNBC personality Jim Cramer, lately. That is even as the Dow Jones Industrial Average was trading more than 350 points higher, with the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite Index both enjoying gains of better-than 1% in early trade (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/global-stocks-dow-futures-regain-ground-as-oil-prices-rebound-2018-11-26).
In a Monday tweet, Cramer appeared to suggest that if the current dynamic walks like a duck and talks like a duck...then it's bear. In other words, if the characteristics of a bear market are on display then the market should consider that one may be at hand.
Indeed, by some measures more than 200 of the S&P 500 index's components and 10 of the Dow's 30 constituents are in a bear market, down at least 20% from a recent bull-market peak, according to FactSet data.
All of the so-called FAANGs, the quintet of growthy stocks that had helped to power this current nearly decade long, bull market higher, including Facebook Inc. (FB), Apple Inc. (AAPL), Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Netflix Inc. (NFLX), and Google-parent Alphabet Inc.(GOOGL) (GOOGL), are in bear market. Bitcoin, arguably the ultimate risk asset, is down 41% this month alone.
To many strategists questioning whether the market is engulfed in bearishness amounts to a pedantic, navel-gazing exercise. That is because, beyond the rule of thumb regarding the degree to which an asset must fall to qualify for a fall into a bear market, there is no ultimate arbiter for corrective market phases, like corrections (a decline of at least 10%) or bear markets.
For many investors, real money has been lost and it isn't clear when the bloodletting will subside.
The CNBC personality, who co-founded the financial news site TheStreet, is best known for a 2007 tirade in which he said of the Fed (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWksEJQEYVU): "They know nothing!" That was a reference to his view that the Fed was ignoring the severity of the asset bubble whose demise was collapsing global financial markets and the U.S. recession that would ensue.
-Mark DeCambre;
 1048ET
